claim: Hematopoietic stem cells emerge during development from vascular components via a process called the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT).
source: Hematopoietic stem cells emerge during development, from vascular components, via a process called the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational concept of the study.

claim: The EHT involves anisotropic contraction along the antero-posterior axis.
source: We show that the transition involves anisotropic contraction along the antero-posterior axis, with heterogenous organization of contractile circumferential actomyosin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The EHT involves heterogenous organization of contractile circumferential actomyosin.
source: We show that the transition involves anisotropic contraction along the antero-posterior axis, with heterogenous organization of contractile circumferential actomyosin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data showing actomyosin organization.

claim: The biomechanics of the EHT contraction is oscillatory.
source: The biomechanics of the contraction is oscillatory, with unusually long periods in comparison to other apical constriction mechanisms described so far in morphogenesis, and is supported by the anisotropic reinforcement of junctional contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis of closing speeds shown in Figure 2.

claim: The EHT has unusually long periods in comparison to other apical constriction mechanisms described in morphogenesis.
source: The biomechanics of the contraction is oscillatory, with unusually long periods in comparison to other apical constriction mechanisms described so far in morphogenesis, and is supported by the anisotropic reinforcement of junctional contacts.
evidence: This comparative claim is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the Discussion section with specific comparisons to other developmental processes.

claim: The EHT is supported by anisotropic reinforcement of junctional contacts.
source: The biomechanics of the contraction is oscillatory, with unusually long periods in comparison to other apical constriction mechanisms described so far in morphogenesis, and is supported by the anisotropic reinforcement of junctional contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ZO1 localization data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Abrogation of blood flow impairs the actin cytoskeleton in EHT cells.
source: Finally, we show that abrogation of blood flow impairs the actin cytoskeleton, the morphodynamics of EHT cells, and the orientation of the emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from silent heart morpholino experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Abrogation of blood flow impairs the morphodynamics of EHT cells.
source: Finally, we show that abrogation of blood flow impairs the actin cytoskeleton, the morphodynamics of EHT cells, and the orientation of the emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by live imaging data from silent heart morpholino experiments.

claim: Abrogation of blood flow impairs the orientation of the emergence.
source: Finally, we show that abrogation of blood flow impairs the actin cytoskeleton, the morphodynamics of EHT cells, and the orientation of the emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by observations that cells can emerge into the aortic lumen when blood flow is abrogated, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Producing full-potential hematopoietic stem cells in vitro remains a challenge.
source: Currently, producing full-potential hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in vitro remains a challenge (Yvernogeau et al., 2016), in particular for regenerative purposes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: HSCs with long-term replenishment potential are formed in the embryo according to a genetic program highly conserved between vertebrate species.
source: HSCs with long-term replenishment potential are formed in the embryo according to a genetic program highly conserved between vertebrate species (Ciau-Uitz et al., 2014; Ciau-Uitz and Patient, 2016; Jaffredo and Yvernogeau, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: HSCs emerge during the definitive wave of hematopoiesis from vascular components, particularly the ventral floor of the dorsal aorta.
source: HSCs emerge during the so-called definitive wave of hematopoiesis, from vascular components, in particular the ventral floor of the dorsal aorta, in the aorta-gonad mesonephros (AGM) region as well as from the umbilical and vitelline arteries in mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about HSC development.

claim: The zebrafish has proven to be an extremely valuable model for studying the developmental aspects of hematopoiesis.
source: The zebrafish has proven to be an extremely valuable model for studying the developmental aspects of hematopoiesis (Frame et al., 2017); the combination of cell tracing and live-imaging have notably allowed to trace the migration of definitive hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to successive hematopoietic organs (Jin et al., 2007; Kissa et al., 2008; Murayama et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the utility of the zebrafish model.

claim: Real-time in vivo imaging established unambiguously the aortic origin of definitive HSPCs.
source: Real-time in vivo imaging also established unambiguously the aortic origin of definitive HSPCs, that were visualized emerging as single cells directly from the hemogenic endothelium in the floor of the dorsal aorta (Bertrand et al., 2010; Kissa and Herbomel, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The EHT is characterized by an unusual bending of the cell that increases while the emergence is progressing.
source: This very unique type of cell emergence, called the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT), is characterized by an unusual bending of the cell that increases while the emergence is progressing, and so until the exit from the vascular wall (Kissa and Herbomel, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: In zebrafish, HSPCs extrude into the sub-aortic space.
source: An apparent difference between zebrafish and mouse is the direction of the emergence, with HSPCs extruding into the sub-aortic space in the former and into the aortic lumen in the latter (where they initiate the so-called intra-aortic clusters).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known difference between species.

claim: In mouse, HSPCs extrude into the aortic lumen where they initiate intra-aortic clusters.
source: An apparent difference between zebrafish and mouse is the direction of the emergence, with HSPCs extruding into the sub-aortic space in the former and into the aortic lumen in the latter (where they initiate the so-called intra-aortic clusters).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known difference between species.

claim: Blood flow appears to regulate endothelial cell fates in development.
source: Blood flow also appears to regulate endothelial cell fates in development (García-Cardeña and Slegtenhorst, 2016) and, in regard to hematopoiesis, to have an influence on the expression of key transcription factors such as Runx1, the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis, both in mouse embryonic stem cells (Adamo et al., 2009) and in the zebrafish (North et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Blood flow has an influence on the expression of Runx1 in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Blood flow also appears to regulate endothelial cell fates in development (García-Cardeña and Slegtenhorst, 2016) and, in regard to hematopoiesis, to have an influence on the expression of key transcription factors such as Runx1, the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis, both in mouse embryonic stem cells (Adamo et al., 2009) and in the zebrafish (North et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Adamo et al., 2009.

claim: Blood flow has an influence on the expression of Runx1 in zebrafish.
source: Blood flow also appears to regulate endothelial cell fates in development (García-Cardeña and Slegtenhorst, 2016) and, in regard to hematopoiesis, to have an influence on the expression of key transcription factors such as Runx1, the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis, both in mouse embryonic stem cells (Adamo et al., 2009) and in the zebrafish (North et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to North et al., 2009.

claim: Runx1 is the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis.
source: Blood flow also appears to regulate endothelial cell fates in development (García-Cardeña and Slegtenhorst, 2016) and, in regard to hematopoiesis, to have an influence on the expression of key transcription factors such as Runx1, the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis, both in mouse embryonic stem cells (Adamo et al., 2009) and in the zebrafish (North et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The EHT allows single live cells to leave a squamous epithelium without perturbing its integrity.
source: The EHT allows single live cells to leave a squamous epithelium without perturbing its integrity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a defining characteristic of the EHT process.

claim: The epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) gives rise to live wandering cells endowed with a new potential, as the EHT does.
source: Most other cell extrusion processes that have been described concern thick, columnar/cuboidal epithelia, and among them, only the epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT, [Lamouille et al., 2014; Nieto et al., 2016]) gives rise to live wandering cells endowed with a new potential, as the EHT does.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the comparison.

claim: The angles of emergence of EHT cells varied between approximately 0–45° from the dorso-ventral axis of the dorsal aorta.
source: We noticed that the angles of emergence of EHT undergoing cells (hereafter designated as 'EHT cells') varied between approximately 0–45° from the dorso-ventral axis of the DA and 0–45° from its antero-posterior (A-P) axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from live imaging.

claim: The angles of emergence of EHT cells varied between approximately 0–45° from the antero-posterior axis of the dorsal aorta.
source: We noticed that the angles of emergence of EHT undergoing cells (hereafter designated as 'EHT cells') varied between approximately 0–45° from the dorso-ventral axis of the DA and 0–45° from its antero-posterior (A-P) axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from live imaging.

claim: The morphological criterion allowing unambiguous identification of cells having initiated the EHT is their cup-shaped morphology, with bending toward the sub-aortic space.
source: As previously described (Kissa and Herbomel, 2010), the morphological criterion allowing unambiguous identification of cells having initiated the EHT is their cup-shaped morphology, with bending toward the sub-aortic space.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: The basal membrane of EHT cells underwent more or less extensive blebbing at the cup-shaped stage.
source: Ras-mCherry allowed visualizing the luminal and basal membranes (Figure 1H), revealing that the latter underwent more or less extensive blebbing at the cup-shaped stage (Figure 1D,I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 1D, H, and I.

claim: Large membrane extensions were formed hours before the cell exit and were reminiscent of cell shape changes occurring during amoeboid migration.
source: This blebbing preceded the protrusion of large membrane extensions that were formed hours before the cell exit and were reminiscent of cell shape changes occuring during amoeboid migration (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by video data.

claim: At the end of the EHT process, a transient narrow membrane foot remained connected to the aorta floor and preceded release in the sub-aortic space.
source: Finally, at the end of the process, Ras-mCherry delineated a transient narrow membrane foot that remained connected to the aorta floor and preceded release in the sub-aortic space (Figure 1F,G and L and Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images and videos.

claim: The time-to-exit from the cup-shaped stage varied widely, with an average duration of 5.48 hr (n = 66).
source: We then measured the time-to-exit, starting from the onset of imaging at the cup-shaped stage and found that it varied widely, with an average duration of 5.48 hr (n = 66, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right panel (note that we define the cup-shaped stage as the steps at which the angle between the axis tangential to the inner cell border and the plane of the aortic floor evolves from 150 to 90°, see A: middle top panel)).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The time intervals between the flat morphology to the cup-shaped stage were very variable, with an average of 6.5 hr (n = 7).
source: The time intervals between the flat morphology to the cup-shaped stage were also very variable, with an average of 6.5 hr (n = 7, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, left panel and Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is little correlation between the A-P luminal distance at the beginning of imaging and the time of exit of the EHT cell.
source: Firstly, we found little correlation between the A-P luminal distance at the beginning of our imaging and the time of exit of the EHT cell (the longest A-P luminal distances did not imply the longest times-to-exit, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of A-P luminal distance measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The narrowing down of the A-P luminal distance did not occur at a uniform pace, but with phases of contraction and of relative stabilization of variable durations.
source: Secondly, we noticed that the narrowing down of the A-P luminal distance did not occur at a uniform pace, but with phases of contraction and of relative stabilization of variable durations taking place in the limit of an A-P luminal distance of approximately 2 µm, followed by steep decrease until the release of the cell (this fast drop may represent a collapse following the culmination of mechanical tensions).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of A-P luminal distance dynamics.

claim: EHT cells maintain contact with their endothelial neighbors until the very end of the process.
source: A specific feature of the EHT is that EHT cells maintain contact with their endothelial neighbors until the very end of the process. This is most probably because of the need to maintain the tightness of the endothelium.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observed feature with a proposed explanation.

claim: There is a heterogeneous density of eGFP-ZO1 at the interfaces between EHT cells and their endothelial neighbors, with an apparent increase at the anterior and posterior poles of the cell.
source: We observed a heterogeneous density of eGFP-ZO1 at the interfaces between EHT cells and their endothelial neighbors, with an apparent increase at the anterior and posterior poles of the cell that persisted until their convergence to apparent coalescence, shortly before cell exit (Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 2A and video.

claim: The eGFP-ZO1 enriched regions at the two opposite poles of the EHT cell moved mainly along the A-P axis, often with an imbalance of migration distance.
source: Firstly, the spots of eGFP-ZO1 high density at the two opposite poles of the EHT cell moved mainly along the A-P axis, often with an imbalance of migration distance (Figure 2B and legend).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by tracking data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The distance between the two eGFP-ZO1 high-density regions decreased non-uniformly with phases of contraction and relative stabilization.
source: Secondly and importantly, the distance between the two eGFP-ZO1 high-density regions decreased non-uniformly (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with phases of contraction and relative stabilization (already visible in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and better resolved spatio-temporally here owing to semi-automatic tracking, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The successive phases of contraction and stabilization are characterized by oscillations of the closing speed with periods of approximately 40 min on average.
source: The successive phases of contraction and stabilization are characterized by oscillations of the closing speed of relatively homogenous periodicity (Figure 2C,D), each oscillation resulting from acceleration and deceleration phases. The oscillations taking place during the contraction phases are the largest in amplitude and are interspersed by short periods of time during which the progression of the A-P distance reaches a minimum (referred to as pseudo-plateaus, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: At 48 hpf, the aortic circumference spans over three cells along most of its length.
source: Firstly, at 48 hpf, as exemplified in Figure 3C–E and Figure 4, the aortic circumference spans over three cells along most of its length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2D-map images in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The aortic cellular landscape is composed of two major populations of cells displaying similar A-P length but different aspect ratio.
source: Secondly, its cellular landscape is composed of two major populations of cells, displaying similar A-P length but a different aspect ratio; one spanning the aortic floor and distinctly narrower in the medio-lateral axis, and the other one spreading across the entire aortic wall, including occasionally the floor (Figure 4B,D and legend).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The laterally narrower cells spanning the aortic floor constitute the hemogenic endothelium.
source: These data support the idea that the laterally narrower cells spanning the aortic floor constitute the hemogenic endothelium.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observation that these cells underwent EHT.

claim: Hemogenic cells are capable of performing mitosis contemporarily to their EHT.
source: Thirdly, hemogenic cells are capable of performing mitosis contemporarily to their EHT, as exemplified in Figure 3C,D in which cell e1 divided symmetrically (based on their morphology) along the A-P axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Mitosis during EHT took place in the aortic plane in 16% of TL sequences.
source: Mitosis during EHT took place in the aortic plane in 16% of our TL sequences, and in the sub-aortic space in 31% of them.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantification of time-lapse sequences.

claim: Mitosis during EHT took place in the sub-aortic space in 31% of TL sequences.
source: Mitosis during EHT took place in the aortic plane in 16% of our TL sequences, and in the sub-aortic space in 31% of them.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantification of time-lapse sequences.

claim: The junctions between EHT cells and their neighbors are characterized by increased density of eGFP-ZO1, particularly at the level of tricellular junctions and contacting surfaces oriented more or less aligned with the medio-lateral axis.
source: Fourthly, the junctions between EHT cells and their neighbors are characterized by increased density of eGFP-ZO1, particularly at the level of tricellular junctions and contacting surfaces that are oriented more or less aligned with the medio-lateral axis (Figure 3C (cells e1 and e2), Figure 4 and Figure 3—video 1, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2D-map images and videos.

claim: At the end of the EHT process, the junctional contacts newly established between adjoining endothelial cells merged into a single line of high eGFP-ZO1 density oriented perpendicular to blood flow.
source: At the end of the process, the junctional contacts newly established between adjoining endothelial cells merged into a single line of high eGFP-ZO1 density oriented perpendicular to blood flow (Video 1, t = 07:00, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 1.

claim: The bijunctional interfaces between endothelial cells that are not in contact with EHT cells and are oriented perpendicular to the A-P axis often exhibit an apparent increase in eGFP-ZO1 density.
source: Fifthly, the bijunctional interfaces between endothelial cells that are not in contact with EHT cells and are oriented perpendicular to the A-P axis also often exhibit an apparent increase in eGFP-ZO1 density (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 4A.

claim: The increase in tight junction components at bi- and tricellular contacts is aimed at reinforcing membrane interfaces that are under high mechanical tension.
source: Hence, we are tempted to deduce that the increase in tight junction components at bi- and tricellular contacts is aimed at reinforcing membrane interfaces that are under high mechanical tension. This would be consistent with the proposed function of tight junctions in the cross-talk with VE-cadherin dependent control of cell-cell tension (Tornavaca et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference with a citation to support the proposed mechanism.

claim: The number of EHT surrounding cells does not vary much during the EHT, with an average of five contacting cells at the beginning, getting down to three at the end of the process.
source: Finally, the number of EHT surrounding cells does not vary much during the EHT, with an average of five contacting cells at the beginning, getting down to three at the end of the process (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lifeact-eGFP was recruited mainly at the cortico-apical side of the EHT cell, assembled as a belt at the interface with its endothelial neighbors with an apparent enrichment at its A and P poles.
source: We observed the recruitment of Lifeact-eGFP mainly at the cortico-apical side of the EHT cell, assembled as a belt at the interface with its endothelial neighbors with an apparent enrichment at its A and P poles (Figure 5A, upper two rows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 5A.

claim: F-actin enrichment at contacting surfaces that are more or less perpendicular to the blood flow is very similar to what was observed with eGFP-ZO1.
source: The 2D-map algorithm revealed F-actin enrichment at contacting surfaces that are more or less perpendicular to the blood flow (Figure 5A, bottom panels). This localization is very similar to what we observed with eGFP-ZO1, suggesting that F-actin contributes to the organization of sub-junctional regions and perhaps the stabilization of junctional complexes that are, as proposed before, the most exposed to mechanical tension.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2D-map images in Figure 5A.

claim: F-actin contributes to the organization of sub-junctional regions and perhaps the stabilization of junctional complexes that are the most exposed to mechanical tension.
source: This localization is very similar to what we observed with eGFP-ZO1, suggesting that F-actin contributes to the organization of sub-junctional regions and perhaps the stabilization of junctional complexes that are, as proposed before, the most exposed to mechanical tension.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observed co-localization of F-actin and ZO1.

claim: The apical constriction of EHT cells requires the contractile activity of a circumferential actomyosin belt.
source: In addition, the data also support the idea that the apical constriction of EHT cells requires the contractile activity of a circumferential actomyosin belt.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the observed F-actin localization and dynamics.

claim: The apical contractile actin belt ultimately shaped into a contractile ring upon the narrowing down of the A-P luminal distance.
source: This confirmed and extended our previous results, showing (i) an apical contractile actin belt that ultimately shaped into a contractile ring upon the narrowing down of the A-P luminal distance and (ii) the subsequent formation of an F-actin enriched foot that preceded the full release of the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on time-lapse imaging of Lifeact-eGFP.

claim: An F-actin enriched foot formed that preceded the full release of the cell.
source: This confirmed and extended our previous results, showing (i) an apical contractile actin belt that ultimately shaped into a contractile ring upon the narrowing down of the A-P luminal distance and (ii) the subsequent formation of an F-actin enriched foot that preceded the full release of the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on time-lapse imaging of Lifeact-eGFP.

claim: The F-actin enriched foot may result from the dissolution of the belt and might serve as a propeller to trigger mechanical force required to complete the exit and/or the mechanical uncoupling of cell-cell junctions.
source: We speculate that this latter pool of F-actin may result from the dissolution of the belt, and might serve as a propeller to trigger mechanical force required to complete the exit and/or the mechanical uncoupling of cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about the function of the F-actin foot.

claim: The anisotropic organization of F-actin and ZO1 in hemogenic and EHT cells suggested that hemodynamic forces may have an influence on the cytoskeleton architecture in these cells as well as on the cytoskeletal/junctional interface.
source: The anisotropic organization of F-actin and ZO1 in hemogenic and EHT cells, with their enrichment at the antero-posterior poles more or less aligned with the blood flow axis, suggested that hemodynamic forces may have an influence on the cytoskeleton architecture in these cells as well as on the cytoskeletal/junctional interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observed anisotropic organization.

claim: The abrogation of heart beating and blood circulation impaired arterial identity and HSC formation in the silent heart (sih) mutant of cardiac troponin T.
source: The involvement of blood flow in hematopoiesis was initially shown in seminal work in the zebrafish (North et al., 2009) in which the abrogation of heart beating and blood circulation impaired arterial identity and HSC formation (using the silent heart (sih) mutant of cardiac troponin T [Sehnert et al., 2002]).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work.

claim: In sih morphants, there was a recurrent absence of EHT cells with cup-shaped morphology and emerging toward the sub-aortic space.
source: We observed, in addition to major alterations in the morphology of the dorsal aorta (Figure 6A), the recurrent absence of EHT cells with cup-shaped morphology and emerging toward the sub-aortic space (14 embryos injected with the sih morpholino were carefully analysed, all along the dorsal aortic wall).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by observations from 14 embryos shown in Figure 6.

claim: In sih morphants, the aortic floor was decorated with ovoid cells, with their luminal/apical membrane protruding into the lumen of the aorta.
source: Rather, the aortic floor was decorated with ovoid cells, with their luminal/apical membrane protruding into the lumen of the aorta (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 6B.

claim: In sih morphants, ovoid cells in the aortic floor are able to emerge either toward the sub-aortic space or toward the aortic lumen.
source: TL sequences performed in the trunk region revealed that the ovoid cells in the aortic floor do undergo mitosis and are able to emerge either toward the sub-aortic space or, more unexpectedly, toward the aortic lumen (Figure 6—video 2, right), which we never saw in the control condition (this intra-aortic emergence was observed in 3/3 movies obtained from three independent injection experiments).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse video data.

claim: In sih morphants, two of the released cells ended up bursting into pieces in one TL sequence.
source: Interestingly, in one of our TL sequences (1/3, the longest TL sequence that lasted 13.30 hr), two of the released cells ended up bursting into pieces (see Figure 6—video 2, left), suggesting that cells released in the absence of mechanical constraints exerted by blood flow are prone to cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by video data.

claim: Cells released in the absence of mechanical constraints exerted by blood flow are prone to cell death.
source: Interestingly, in one of our TL sequences (1/3, the longest TL sequence that lasted 13.30 hr), two of the released cells ended up bursting into pieces (see Figure 6—video 2, left), suggesting that cells released in the absence of mechanical constraints exerted by blood flow are prone to cell death. This is consistent with previous studies showing a reduction in the number of hematopoietic stem cells and progenitors upon sih morpholino treatment (in particular in the caudal hematopoietic tissue, see Murayama et al., 2006; Murayama et al. (2006); Bertrand et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from observed cell bursting, with citations to support the interpretation.

claim: Hemodynamic mechanical forces contribute to the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane of EHT cells (the cup-shaped cells) as well as the direction of the emergence (toward the sub-aortic space).
source: Altogether, these results support the idea that hemodynamic mechanical forces contribute to the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane of EHT cells (the cup-shaped cells) as well as the direction of the emergence (toward the sub-aortic space).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the sih morpholino experiments.

claim: The biomechanics of the emergence may impact downstream cellular functions and/or commitments that, if not fulfilled, impede cell survival.
source: They also suggest that the biomechanics of the emergence may impact downstream cellular functions and/or commitments that, if not fulfilled, impede cell survival.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observation of cell death in sih morphants.

claim: When heart beating and blood flow were temporarily arrested using tricaine, the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane was not observed anymore and cells performing the emergence toward the sub-aortic space maintained their path.
source: Interestingly, when heart beating and blood flow were temporarily arrested using tricaine methanesulfonate (at 1 mg/ml), the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane was not observed anymore and cells performing the emergence toward the sub-aortic space maintained their path (10 embryos were observed, all along the dorsal aortic wall, between a time window of 35–135 min after interruption of blood flow, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from 10 embryos.

claim: Components of hemodynamic forces (among which the mechanical strain, the force perpendicular to the flow axis acting on the vascular wall) are exerting a direct action on the apical/luminal membrane bending.
source: This result strongly supports the idea that components of hemodynamic forces (among which the mechanical strain, the force perpendicular to the flow axis acting on the vascular wall) are exerting a direct action on the apical/luminal membrane bending.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the tricaine experiment.

claim: Obliterating blood flow revealed a perturbation of F-actin organization in EHT cells, with little reinforcement of that staining at the antero-posterior poles of the cells in comparison to the control.
source: Images clearly revealed a perturbation of F-actin organization in EHT cells, with little reinforcement of that staining at the antero-posterior poles of the cells in comparison to the control (Figure 6B, bottom panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 2D-map images in Figure 6B.

claim: Obliterating blood flow revealed changes in eGFP-ZO1 localization in cells of the hemogenic endothelium, with altered recruitment at the sub-plasmalemmal level and apparent increase of the eGFP-ZO1 cytoplasmic pool.
source: However, 3D-projections and 3D-analysis with the Imaris software also revealed changes in eGFP-ZO1 localization in cells of the hemogenic endothelium, with altered recruitment at the sub-plasmalemmal level and apparent increase of the eGFP-ZO1 cytoplasmic pool (Figure 6C and see Figure 6—video 3 for 3D-Imaris rendering).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by 3D images in Figure 6C and video.

claim: Hemodynamic forces exert an action on the cytoskeletal architecture of hemogenic cells and impact on junctional organization.
source: Altogether, these results support the idea that hemodynamic forces exert an action on the cytoskeletal architecture of hemogenic cells and impact on junctional organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the blood flow abrogation experiments.

claim: The A and P neighbors of EHT cells moved toward each other over the actin-rich poles and appeared to extend actin-rich filopodia to establish contacts.
source: Time-lapse imaging of Lifeact-eGFP in embryos in which the EHT cells were best aligned with the A-P axis also suggested an active role of the adjoining endothelial cells in the process. The A and P neighbors moved toward each other over the actin-rich poles and appeared to extend actin-rich filopodia to establish contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: Filopodia anastomosis should contribute to the sealing of the aorta floor.
source: Subsequently, filopodia anastomosis should contribute to the sealing of the aorta floor (Figure 7—video 1, with the main sequential steps composing Figure 7, left panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from observed filopodia dynamics.

claim: The myl9 gene was shown to be a target of Runx1 in a genome-wide analysis of the transcriptional profile and of Runx1 binding in a model of the mouse hemogenic endothelium in cell culture.
source: We focused on the regulatory light chain 9 (Myl9) because the myl9 gene was shown to be a target of Runx1 in a genome-wide analysis of the transcriptional profile and of Runx1 binding in a model of the mouse hemogenic endothelium in cell culture (Lie-A-Ling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: The myl9 gene was duplicated in the zebrafish, leading to the expression of two paralogs bearing more than 93% identity and referred to as Myl9a and Myl9b.
source: Owing to gene duplication in teleosts, the myl9 gene was duplicated in the zebrafish, leading to the expression of two paralogs bearing more than 93% identity and referred to as Myl9a and Myl9b (for sequence comparison, see Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The myl9a mRNA is expressed in the dorsal aorta of 48 hpf embryos.
source: By WISH, we confirmed that the myl9a mRNA is expressed in the dorsal aorta of 48 hpf embryos (Figure 8A) and we found that so is the case for myl9b.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization images in Figure 8A.

claim: The myl9b mRNA is expressed in the dorsal aorta of 48 hpf embryos.
source: By WISH, we confirmed that the myl9a mRNA is expressed in the dorsal aorta of 48 hpf embryos (Figure 8A) and we found that so is the case for myl9b. More precisely, we detected the myl9b mRNA in the brain, somites, and dorsal aorta (owing to strong signals in the ventral part of the somites, transverse sectioning was necessary to visualize unambiguously the localization of myl9b mRNA in aortic cells, Figure 8A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization images in Figure 8A.

claim: Knock-down of Myl9a resulted in a significant decrease in HSPC number in the AGM and the CHT.
source: In both knock-downs, we observed a significant decrease in HSPC number in the AGM and the CHT (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Knock-down of Myl9b resulted in a significant decrease in HSPC number in the AGM and the CHT.
source: In both knock-downs, we observed a significant decrease in HSPC number in the AGM and the CHT (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 8D and E.

claim: The phenotype of decreased HSPC number was phenocopied by two additional morpholinos targeting myl9b and myl9a mRNAs respectively and was rescued for the spe3i3 myl9b morpholino.
source: This phenotype was phenocopied by two additional morpholinos targeting myl9b and myl9a mRNAs respectively and was rescued for the spe3i3 myl9b morpholino (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both Myl9a and Myl9b are involved in definitive hematopoiesis, and possibly in the EHT process.
source: These data support the involvement of both Myl9a and Myl9b in definitive hematopoiesis, and possibly in the EHT process.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the morpholino knock-down experiments.

claim: Myl9a-eGFP and Myl9b-eGFP assemble as cortico-apical belts with enrichment at spots between EHT cells and neighbors that move, upon apical constriction, along the A-P axis, and coalesce.
source: However, as seen in Video 2, regular TL sequences show convincingly that Myl9a-eGFP and Myl9b-eGFP assemble as cortico-apical belts with enrichment at spots between EHT cells and neighbors that move, upon apical constriction, along the A-P axis, and coalesce.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 2.

claim: The dynamics of Myl9a and Myl9b belts/rings is reminiscent of what was observed with Lifeact-eGFP and eGFP-ZO1.
source: This is reminiscent of what we observed with Lifeact-eGFP and eGFP-ZO1 (see Video 3 for a comparative 'en face' visualization of the dynamics of actin and myosin belts/rings).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 3.

claim: Myl9a and Myl9b were recruited at the contracting cytokinesis ring in EHT cells that underwent mitosis.
source: We also noticed that Myl9a and b were recruited at the contracting cytokinesis ring in EHT cells that underwent mitosis (see Video 2 and its legend).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 2.

claim: The most significant difference between Myl9b and Myl9a resides in their amino-terminus, where the two serines following the starting methionine are present in Myl9b, but not in Myl9a.
source: Myl9b and Myl9a are very similar (93% identity calculated by ClustalO), and the most significant difference resides in their amino-terminus, where the two serines following the starting methionine (which are strictly conserved in mammals and in most zebrafish RLCs, see Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) are present in Myl9b, but not in Myl9a.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two amino-terminal serine residues in Myl9b are the substrates of protein kinase C (PKC) activity.
source: These two residues are the substrates of protein kinase C (PKC) activity (Ikebe et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of the amino-terminal serines impairs the phosphorylation of the downstream Rho-kinase/MLCK/Citron-kinase target site that is essential for the stimulatory activity of RLCs on the ATPase activity of the myosin heavy chain.
source: It was shown that their phosphorylation impairs the phosphorylation of the downstream Rho-kinase/MLCK/Citron-kinase target site (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) that is essential for the stimulatory activity of RLCs on the ATPase activity of the myosin heavy chain (Turbedsky et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of the amino-terminal site inhibits myosin activity and actomyosin contraction.
source: Hence, phosphorylation of this amino-terminal site inhibits myosin activity and actomyosin contraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the known effects of phosphorylation.

claim: Expression of the Myl9bA2A3 mutant form using the kdrl promoter caused mild morphological alterations of the dorsal vascular system.
source: Expression of the mutant form using the kdrl promoter caused mild morphological alterations of the dorsal vascular system (with maintenance of blood flow, no obvious change in the shape of the dorsal aorta and a few distortions at the base of intersegmental vessels, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations.

claim: At 40 and 50 hpf, in comparison with the wt form, there was a much lower number of HSPCs expressing the Myl9bA2A3 mutant form, both in the sub-aortic space and in the CHT.
source: At 40 and 50 hpf, and in comparison with the wt form, we found a much lower number of HSPCs expressing the mutant form, both in the sub-aortic space and in the CHT (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 9A and B.

claim: Preventing N-terminal phosphorylation impairs definitive hematopoiesis and may interfere with the emergence from the aortic floor.
source: These results suggest that preventing N-terminal phosphorylation impairs definitive hematopoiesis and may interfere with the emergence from the aortic floor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the Myl9bA2A3 mutant phenotype.

claim: Hemogenic cells in the aortic floor that expressed the wt Myl9b-eGFP occasionally underwent EHT, but such cells were not found upon expressing Myl9bA2A3-eGFP.
source: Firstly, while we occasionally found hemogenic cells in the aortic floor that expressed the wt Myl9b-eGFP and underwent EHT, we were unable to find such cells upon expressing Myl9bA2A3-eGFP, suggesting that the latter cells emerged at a significantly lesser frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on live imaging observations.

claim: Cellular fragments were often seen in the sub-aortic area in Myl9bA2A3-eGFP expressing embryos, usually indicative of cell bursting.
source: Secondly, cellular fragments were often seen in the sub-aortic area, usually indicative of cell bursting. This cell fragmentation may have occurred during the EHT as described upon runx1 knock-down (Kissa and Herbomel, 2010), or in EHT-derived HSPCs as upon scl-α knock-down (Zhen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work showing similar phenotypes.

claim: EHT-derived HSPCs expressing Myl9bA2A3-eGFP exhibited abnormal shapes and migration, characterized by anarchic membrane extensions in many directions at once.
source: Thirdly, EHT-derived HSPCs expressing Myl9bA2A3-eGFP exhibited abnormal shapes and migration, characterized by anarchic membrane extensions in many directions at once (Figure 9D and Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 9D and video.

claim: EHT-derived HSPCs expressing Myl9bA2A3-eGFP were still able to undergo mitosis, with Myl9bA2A3 relocating to the cytokinesis ring as wt Myl9b would do.
source: Interestingly, they were still able to undergo mitosis, with Myl9bA2A3 relocating to the cytokinesis ring as wt Myl9b would do (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations.

claim: The inward bending of the luminal membrane of EHT cells is one of the hallmarks of the EHT that has never been described for any other type of cell extrusion.
source: The inward bending of the luminal membrane of EHT cells is one of the hallmarks of the EHT that, to our knowledge, has never been described so far for any other type of cell extrusion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a unique feature of the EHT.

claim: Electron microscopic images of cells of the embryonic mouse aorta floor showed the presence of large intracellular vacuole-like structures reminiscent of what is observed in the zebrafish embryo.
source: Indeed, electron microscopic images of cells of the embryonic mouse aorta floor showed the presence of large intracellular vacuole-like structures (Marshall and Thrasher, 2001) reminiscent of what is observed in the zebrafish embryo, raising the idea that the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane may be followed by its intracellular release after the emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to prior work.

claim: The inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane may be followed by its intracellular release after the emergence.
source: Indeed, electron microscopic images of cells of the embryonic mouse aorta floor showed the presence of large intracellular vacuole-like structures (Marshall and Thrasher, 2001) reminiscent of what is observed in the zebrafish embryo, raising the idea that the inward bending of the apical/luminal membrane may be followed by its intracellular release after the emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on comparative observations.

claim: The variation in the direction of emergence between the mouse and the zebrafish may be a direct consequence of differences in the strength of components of hemodynamic forces, such as the mechanical strain.
source: Unless, in the zebrafish, hemogenic cells that have never been exposed to hemodynamic forces do not express the relevant cytosolic machineries essential for performing a sub-aortic emergence, this raises the possibility that the variation between the two species is a direct consequence of differences in the strength of components of hemodynamic forces, such as, for example, the mechanical strain (the force perpendicular to the direction of the flow and that relates to the rhythm of heart beating, Hahn and Schwartz, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis with a citation.

claim: The physical properties of the respective aortic walls might impact the way they respond to hemodynamic forces because of their diameters, much wider in the mouse than in the zebrafish.
source: Hence, it is not so clear if the sub-aortic orientation of the emergence of HSCs in the zebrafish may be a direct consequence of the mechanical strain; what might count as well regarding the difference between the two species are the physical properties of the respective aortic walls that should impact the way they respond to the force because of their diameters, much wider in the mouse than in the zebrafish (approximately 300 μm in the mouse and 25 μm in the zebrafish embryos at the time window of the EHT).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Young aortic cells (at 48 hpf) are more exposed to tension than 2 days later, when the aorta has matured and the aortic cells align with the direction of the flow.
source: Indeed, it has been shown by using a VE-cadherin mechanical sensor, that young aortic cells (at 48 hpf), are more exposed to tension than 2 days later, when the aorta has matured and the aortic cells align with the direction of the flow (Lagendijk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to prior work.

claim: Elongated hemogenic and EHT cells, on the aortic floor, may orientate and contract along the A-P axis to minimize environmental constraints and membrane tension.
source: Hence, elongated hemogenic and EHT cells, on the aortic floor, may also orientate and contract along that same axis (as we show in our work with the 2D-maping results), to minimize environmental constraints and membrane tension.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the observed orientation and the known mechanical environment.

claim: The membrane interfaces that remain the most exposed to mechanical tensions are most probably the ones that are enriched in ZO1 and actin and are oriented perpendicular to blood flow.
source: In this context, the membrane interfaces that remain the most exposed to mechanical tensions are most probably the ones that are enriched in ZO1 and actin and are oriented perpendicular to blood flow (consistently with ZO1 enrichment at the interface between endothelial cells that spread over a large surface of the aorta and whose orientation is also perpendicular to blood flow).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the observed ZO1 and actin localization.

claim: Tensions exerted by the hemodynamics control sub-plasmalemmal cytoskeletal architecture in EHT cells and, consequently, the actin/junctional interface.
source: According to our results obtained upon abrogation of heart beating and showing alteration of actin anisotropy (i.e the reduction in the recruitment of sub-cortical actin at the two poles of the cells more or less aligned with the blood flow axis), tensions exerted by the hemodynamics control sub-plasmalemmal cytoskeletal architecture in EHT cells and, consequently, the actin/junctional interface (as suggested by the delocalization of ZO1 that we observe in these conditions).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the blood flow abrogation experiments.

claim: The EHT biomechanics are specifically adapted to - and influenced by - the mechanical tensions exerted by blood flow.
source: Altogether, these results support the conclusion that the EHT biomechanics are specifically adapted to - and influenced by - the mechanical tensions exerted by blood flow.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The control of EHT biomechanics by blood flow might be direct (ex: via cell surface mechanosensors), and/or indirect (ex: via the induction of Runx1).
source: It should be noted that this control by the flow might be direct (ex: via cell surface mechanosensors), and/or indirect (ex: via the induction of Runx1, the transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis [Adamo et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as possible mechanisms with a citation.

claim: Hemodynamics and in particular shear stress was shown to control endothelial cell morphology and influence the expression of many transcription factors.
source: Indeed, hemodynamics and in particular shear stress was shown to control endothelial cell morphology and influence the expression of many transcription factors (for example, for a link between flow, mechanotransduction, actin, transcription see Nakajima et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to prior work.

claim: The constriction of the apical/luminal side of EHT cells should depend on the activity of actomyosin recruited at the junctional circumferential belt.
source: The constriction of the apical/luminal side of EHT cells, like many apical cell constriction events described so far, should depend on the activity of actomyosin recruited at the junctional circumferential belt.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on comparison to other apical constriction mechanisms.

claim: The membrane interfaces that are the less enriched in actomyosin (oriented along the antero-posterior axis) are the ones that shrink the most, supporting the idea that the constriction is also coupled with their consumption, possibly by endocytosis.
source: The membrane interfaces that are the less enriched in actomyosin (oriented along the antero-posterior axis), are the ones that shrink the most, supporting the idea that the constriction is also coupled with their consumption, possibly by endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the observed actomyosin distribution and membrane dynamics.

claim: The average period of oscillations during EHT apical constriction is approximately 40 min, which is longer than in other extensively studied developmental processes.
source: This average period value is longer than in the most extensively studied and quantified processes taking place during development, such as, for example, the apical-medial contraction of cells during ventral mesoderm invagination in Drosophila melanogaster embryos (see the seminal article [Martin et al., 2009]), or the apical-medial and apical-junctional mediated contractions during neuroblasts ingression (see [An et al., 2017; Simões et al., 2017]); the latter being more comparable to the EHT process since a single cell extrudes from an epithelium, the ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to comparative studies.

claim: The specific parameters of the oscillations of the apical closing speed for EHT cells correlate with the time scale of the whole process, suggesting that they may be controlled at the mesoscopic level, perhaps involving gene regulatory networks controlling cyclic expression of genes.
source: This suggests that the specific parameters of the oscillations of the apical closing speed for EHT cells that impact on contraction efficiencies (in particular for periods and amplitudes) correlate with the time scale of the whole process, suggesting that they may be controlled at the mesoscopic level, perhaps involving gene regulatory networks controlling cyclic expression of genes (such as in the case of ultradian oscillations that have periods in the time-range of the hour, see Isomura and Kageyama, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis with a citation.

claim: EHT cells are integrated into a developing lumenized tissue that is submitted to a series of mechanical tensions owing to aortic morphological maturation.
source: Indeed, EHT cells are integrated into a developing lumenized tissue that is submitted to a series of mechanical tensions owing to aortic morphological maturation including (i) the adaptation of the endothelial wall to EHT cell emergence and the significant reduction of the aortic diameter with time (Isogai et al., 2001; Kissa and Herbomel, 2010; Sugden et al., 2017), (ii) the extensive modification of the structure of the sub-aortic space (with the modification of the basal lamina contacting EHT cells and transducing forces via integrins; see the incidence of basal lamina on periods of oscillations [Gorfinkiel, 2016; Koride et al., 2014]) and, last but not least, (iii) complex hemodynamic forces.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations to support the various sources of mechanical tension.

claim: High mechanical tensions might tune the downstream molecular events controlling actin-driven directional forces and actomyosin recruitment and contractility.
source: In such environment, the high mechanical tensions might tune the downstream molecular events controlling actin-driven directional forces and actomyosin recruitment and contractility (for the relevance of high-order information, at the tissue level, on the biomechanics and role of contractile pulses and the theoretical description of pulsatile/oscillatory behaviour, see [Levayer and Lecuit, 2012]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis with a citation.

claim: A major regulatory axis of the EHT process relies on controlling actomyosin activity, by regulating a complex interplay between activating and inhibitory kinases.
source: Hence, this reinforces the possibility that a major regulatory axis of the EHT process relies on controlling actomyosin activity, by regulating a complex interplay between activating and inhibitory kinases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the Myl9b mutagenesis results.

claim: Myl9b, via the phosphorylation of its N-terminus, may contribute to the tuning of the mechanical parameters of the contraction.
source: In this scenario, there exists the possibility that Myl9b, via the phosphorylation of its N-terminus, contributes to the tuning of the mechanical parameters of the contraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis about Myl9b function.

claim: Myl9a may be co-expressed with Myl9b in EHT cells, and since the knock-down of myl9a impairs definitive hematopoiesis, both isoforms may be involved in the EHT, with a fine tuning of their molecular ratio.
source: Finally, there may be additional complexity to the system, for another RLC, Myl9a, is expressed in the aorta and may be co-expressed with Myl9b in EHT cells. Myl9a is a paralog that appears to be more restricted to the zebrafish and lacks the N-terminal, PKC phosphorylation site. Since the knock-down of myl9a, as is the case for myl9b, impairs definitive hematopoiesis, both isoforms may be involved in the EHT, with a fine tuning of their molecular ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis about the roles of both Myl9 isoforms.
